changes.summary: The Menil Collection stewards a significant collection of more than 300 works from the Pacific Islands. Masks, figural sculptures, architectural elements, and musical instruments, primarily from the regions of Melanesia and Polynesia, are regularly on view in a dedicated gallery and in A Surrealist Wunderkammer. A slit gong (atingting kon) and tree fern grade figures (mage or bwerang) from Vanuatu occupy the center of the Pacific Islands gallery. The display emulates the ceremonial space or clearing (nasara) in which name- or title-taking rituals take place on the islands of Ambrym and Malakula. This grouping of monumental works also denotes a separation between the display objects from Polynesia and Melanesia, which are on opposite sides of the gallery. One section highlights the sophisticated wood carving of Polynesia with a “treasure box” (papahou) from the Māori and an incredibly rare drum (pahu ra) from the Austral Islands. Commemorative arts from Papua New Guinea and the neighboring island of New Ireland represent the visual culture of Melanesia. The memorial figure (uli) and vertical ceremonial pole (valik ekuar) on view are examples associated with the central New Ireland funerary traditions of malagan, which includes multiple weeks of communal exchanges of carvings, masks, and pigs. The Pacific Islands objects held by the museum are among the earliest collected by John and Dominique de Menil. In 1924, John de Menil was one of seven students selected by the French government and the Parisian Le Journal for a sponsored tour around the world. During his six-month long voyage, which included brief stays in Vanuatu, Tahiti, and Fiji, he collected examples of local textiles. In 1932, the de Menils purchased two painted bark textiles (maro) from French Surrealist Jacques Viot, who had recently returned from a collecting expedition in the Humboldt Bay and Lake Sentani regions of Papua, Indonesia.
